t.4.11.1: Having heard Rāma's words, which increased his joy and his courage, Sugrīva honored Rāghava and praised him.
t.4.11.2: Without doubt, if you were enraged, you could burn up the worlds with your blazing, sharp arrows that pierce the vitals, like the sun at the end of the age.
t.4.11.3: Hear from me with undivided mind what Vālin's manly prowess is, and what his valour and his fortitude are; then decide what is to be done next.
t.4.11.5: Climbing to the tops of the mountains, the mighty one swiftly hurls even their huge peaks upward and catches them again.
t.4.11.4: Before the sun has risen, Vālī, free from all weariness, strides from the western ocean to the eastern, and from the southern to the northern.
t.4.11.6: Many sturdy trees of various kinds in the forests have been broken by Vālin with his force, as he displayed his own strength.
t.4.11.7: There was a buffalo named Dundubhi, radiant like a peak of Kailāsa; that mighty one possessed the strength of a thousand elephants.
t.4.11.8: Puffed up with pride in his own strength and deluded by the granting of a boon, that wicked-souled one of mighty body went to the ocean, lord of the rivers.
t.4.11.9: Disregarding the wave-filled ocean, that treasury of gems, he said to the great sea, "Give me battle!"
t.4.11.10: Then the mighty Ocean, righteous of soul, rose up and spoke these words, O king, to the asura who was driven on by Time.
t.4.11.11: I am not able to give you battle, O you who are skilled in battle. Listen, I shall tell you of the one who will give you battle.
t.4.11.12: In the great forest stands the king of mountains, the supreme refuge of ascetics, the father-in-law of Śaṃkara, renowned by the name Himavān.
t.4.11.13: Furnished with caves and springs, with many caverns and waterfalls, he is able to give you matchless delight in battle.
t.4.11.14: Perceiving that the ocean was afraid, the foremost of asuras went to the forest of Himavat, like an arrow loosed from a bow.
t.4.11.15: Then Dundubhi hurled down to the ground, in many ways, the white rocks of that mountain, huge as lordly elephants, and he roared aloud.
t.4.11.16: Then Himavān, gentle and of a form that gave delight, shaped like a white cloud, spoke these words while standing upon his own peak.
t.4.11.17: O Dundubhi, you who cherish dharma, you ought not to harass me, for I am unskilled in the deeds of battle; I am a refuge for ascetics.
t.4.11.18: Having heard those words of the wise king of mountains, Dundubhi, his eyes reddened with anger, spoke these words.
t.4.11.19: If you are incapable in battle, or have lost all resolve out of fear of me, then name to me the one who would give me battle today, for I am eager to fight.
t.4.11.20: Having heard the words spoken in anger, the righteous Himavān, skilled in speech, addressed that foremost of asuras with words he had never spoken before.
t.4.11.21: A glorious monkey named Vālī, greatly wise and equal in valour to Śakra, dwells in Kiṣkindhā, a city of matchless splendour.
t.4.11.22: He, greatly wise and skilled in battle, is able to give you a great single combat, as Vāsava gave to Namuci.
t.4.11.23: Go to him quickly, if you desire battle here, for he is ever hard to overcome, a hero in the work of war.
t.4.11.24: Having heard the words of Himavant, that Dundubhi, possessed by rage, then went to Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālin.
t.4.11.25: Assuming the form of a buffalo, sharp-horned and terrifying, he looked like a great cloud full of water in the sky in the rainy season.
t.4.11.26: Then the mighty Dundubhi, reaching the gate of Kiṣkindhā, roared, making the earth tremble, as though with the booming of drums.
t.4.11.28: Vālī, who was in the inner apartments, heard the sound and, unable to bear it, rushed out together with his women, like the moon with the stars.
t.4.11.27: Breaking the trees that grew nearby, rending the earth with his hooves, and in his arrogance gouging that gate with his horn, like an elephant.
t.4.11.29: Vālī, lord of the monkeys and of all the forest-dwellers, spoke to that Dundubhi in measured words, with clear syllables and phrases.
t.4.11.30: Why do you roar, having blocked this gate of the city? Dundubhi, you are known to me; save your life, O mighty one.
t.4.11.31: Having heard those words of the wise lord of the vānaras, Dundubhi, his eyes reddened with anger, spoke these words.
t.4.11.32: You ought not to speak such words in the presence of women, O hero. Give me battle, and then I shall know your strength.
t.4.11.33: Or else I shall hold back my anger today, for this one night; until the sunrise, O monkey, indulge yourself freely in the pleasures of desire.
t.4.11.34: Whoever kills one who is drunk, or careless, or asleep, or utterly defenceless, someone like you, deluded by intoxication, is held in the world to be a slayer of an unborn child.
t.4.11.35: Then, having sent away all those women headed by Tārā, he laughed softly and, in anger, spoke to that foremost of asuras.
t.4.11.36: Do not think, 'This one is drunk,' if you are truly fearless in battle; in this encounter, let this intoxication be regarded as the draught that heroes drink before fighting.
t.4.11.37: Having spoken thus to him, the enraged one lifted up the golden garland given to him by his father, the great Indra, and stood firm, ready for battle.
t.4.11.38: Seizing by the horns that Dundubhi, who resembled a mountain, Vālī struck him down and roared with a mighty roar.
t.4.11.39: In that life-taking fight Dundubhi was then crushed, and as he was being hurled down, blood streamed from his ears. And that huge-bodied one fell upon the earth, having met his death.
t.4.11.40: Lifting him with both arms, lifeless and senseless, the mighty Vālī hurled him with a single heave a full yojana away.
t.4.11.41: From the mouth of him, hurled with great force, drops of blood fell, borne up by the wind, toward the hermitage of Mataṃga.
t.4.11.42: Seeing those drops of blood fallen there, the sage hurled a great curse at Vālin, the one who had thrown the carcass: "He must not enter here; should he enter, death would be his." He, approaching the great sage, entreated him with joined palms.
t.4.11.43: Therefore, frightened by fear of the curse, the monkey does not wish to enter the great mountain Ṛśyamūka, or even to look at it, O lord of men.
t.4.11.44: Knowing that he cannot enter here, O Rāma, I wander through this great forest together with my ministers, free from despondency.
t.4.11.46: And here are these seven mighty sāla trees with their drooping branches, any one of which Vālī, by his strength, strives to strip bare of its leaves.
t.4.11.45: This great heap of bones, looking like a mountain peak, is clearly visible here: it belongs to that Dundubhi, who was flung away in an outburst of overweening strength.
t.4.11.47: This matchless valour of his has been made known by me, O Rāma. How will you be able to slay that Vālin in battle, O king?
t.4.11.48: If you, O mighty-armed one, could pierce these sāla trees with a single arrow, then I would know you to be capable of slaying Vālin.
t.4.11.49: Having heard those words of the great-souled Sugrīva, the mighty-armed Rāghava playfully lifted the body of Dundubhi with his big toe and hurled it ten yojanas away.
t.4.11.50: Then, having seen the body hurled away, Sugrīva again spoke these meaningful words to Rāma in front of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.11.51: Friend, when it was thrown long ago, the body was moist, full of flesh and fresh; now, Rāghava, it is light, fleshless and has become like straw. So from this it cannot be known whether your strength or his is greater.
